m = d/z in mm; circular pitch p = πm; base pitch πm cos φ
Angle between the line of action and the common tangent of the pitch circles; 20° standard; d<sub>b</sub> = d cos φ
Path of contact ÷ base pitch; must exceed 1 (1.67 for z = 20/60, m = 4)
K = 0.16(BHN/100)² N/mm² for a steel pair; the wear strength is proportional to it

takeaways: A gear pair runs at a truly constant ratio because the involute keeps the common normal fixed through the pitch point; the contact ratio says how many teeth share the load.
A gear material is a package: a tough core for root bending and a hard surface for pitting, with the pinion harder because it sees ratio-times more cycles.
Lewis sizes the module (S<sub>b</sub> = σ<sub>b</sub> b m Y with a velocity factor); Buckingham then checks the same tooth for dynamic load and wear, and either check can govern.
Helical gears are designed on the normal section with z<sub>v</sub> = z/cos³ψ; they run quieter and carry more, but push the shaft with F<sub>t</sub> tan ψ.
Bevel teeth are designed as spur teeth on the back cone (z<sub>v</sub> = z/cos γ), with the load at the mean radius and the taper factor (1 − b/R).
In a worm drive the lead angle sets the efficiency; friction heat, not tooth strength, usually limits a worm box.
Epicyclic trains are solved by holding the arm, then adding the arm's motion; a fixed member carries a holding torque but no power.
Gear life is counted in cycles; a load spectrum becomes one equivalent load through Miner's rule, and the gearbox is then checked for ratio split, bearings and heat.
A multi-speed gearbox multiplies group ratios; the ray diagram shows every speed and ratio, and tooth numbers follow from equal tooth sums in each group.
bank_note: Long answers in most syllabi are a full design in sequence: geometry, material, Lewis sizing with a velocity factor, then the Buckingham dynamic and wear checks (or efficiency and heat for a worm), ending with the check that governs. Gear trains and ray diagrams are asked as calculations with a table or a sketch.

bank.q: State the law of gearing. With a neat sketch of two involute teeth in contact, show that the common normal at the point of contact always passes through the pitch point, and hence that the angular velocity ratio stays constant throughout the mesh.
outline: Statement: the common normal at the point of contact must pass through a fixed pitch point P on the line of centres
Proof: velocities along the common normal are equal, similar triangles give ω<sub>1</sub>/ω<sub>2</sub> = O<sub>2P</sub>/O<sub>1P</sub>
Involute property: its normal is tangent to the base circle
For two involutes the common normal is the fixed common tangent of the base circles, so P is fixed and the ratio constant
Bonus: ratio unchanged by a small change of centre distance

answer.text: Statement. For two gears to turn at a constant angular velocity ratio, the common normal to the tooth profiles at the point of contact must always pass through a fixed point P on the line of centres O1O_{2}. P is the pitch point, where the two pitch circles touch.

Sketch. Draw centres O1 (pinion) and O2 (gear), the line of centres, the two pitch circles touching at P, the two base circles, and two involute flanks touching at a point C. Through C draw the common tangent and the common normal N1N_{2}; mark the feet of the perpendiculars from O1 and O2 on the normal as N1 and N2.
answer.pre:
O<sub>1</sub> ●
       \  N<sub>1</sub>
        \ /
   ------P------  common tangent of the pitch circles
        / \
      N<sub>2</sub>   (line N<sub>1</sub>-C-N<sub>2</sub> is the common normal)
O<sub>2</sub> ●

answer.text: Velocities at C. As part of the pinion, C moves with v1 = ω1 · O1C, perpendicular to O1C. As part of the gear, it moves with v2 = ω2 · O2C, perpendicular to O2C. The two profiles stay in contact without digging into each other or separating, so their velocity components along the common normal must be equal: v1 cos α1 = v2 cos α2, where α1 and α2 are the angles between each velocity and the normal.

Turning that into the ratio. v1 cos α1 = ω1 · O1C cos α1 = ω1 · O1N_1, because O1N_1 is the projection of O1C perpendicular to the normal. In the same way v2 cos α2 = ω2 · O2N_{2}. Hence ω1 · O1N_1 = ω2 · O2N_2 and ω1/ω2 = O2N_2/O1N_{1}.

Similar triangles. Triangles O1N_1P and O2N_2P are similar (right angles at N1 and N2, equal vertical angles at P), so O2N_2/O1N_1 = O2P/O1P. Therefore ω1/ω2 = O2P/O1P. The ratio is constant only if P is a fixed point, which is the law of gearing.

The involute satisfies it. An involute is traced by the end of a taut string unwound from the base circle, so its normal at any point is the string itself, tangent to the base circle. At C the normal to the pinion flank is tangent to the pinion base circle and the normal to the gear flank is tangent to the gear base circle. Both are the same line, so the common normal is the common internal tangent N1N_2 of the two base circles.

The normal is fixed in space. The base circles do not move as the gears turn, so their common tangent is the same line at every instant. Contact moves along this line (the line of action), and the line always cuts O1O_2 at the same point P. Hence ω1/ω2 = O2P/O1P = r2/r1 = rb2/rb1 = z2/z1 at every position of the mesh.

Check with numbers. For the pair z1 = 20, z2 = 60, m = 4 mm: rb1 = 37.59 mm and rb2 = 112.76 mm, and 112.76/37.59 = 3.00 = 60/20. If the centre distance is opened from 160 to 160.5 mm, the base radii do not change, so the ratio stays 3.00; only the working pressure angle rises (cos φ′ = 160 cos 20°/160.5, φ′ = 20.5°) and the backlash grows. This tolerance is why involute teeth are standard.

bank.q: Define module, circular pitch, diametral pitch, pressure angle, addendum, dedendum, backlash and contact ratio for a spur gear pair. Give the relations between module, circular pitch and number of teeth, and state the standard pressure angle.
outline: m = d/z in mm; p = πm; P = z/d (inch), m = 25.4/P
Pressure angle between line of action and common tangent at P; 20° standard
Addendum m, dedendum 1.25m for 20° full depth
Backlash: gap between non-driving flanks
Contact ratio = path of contact/base pitch, above 1

answer.text: Module m = d/z, the pitch circle diameter per tooth, in mm (d in mm, z the number of teeth). Standard first-choice modules are 1, 1.25, 1.5, 2, 2.5, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8 and 10 mm.
Circular pitch p: the distance from a point on one tooth to the same point on the next, measured along the pitch circle: p = πd/z = πm. For m = 4 mm, p = 12.57 mm.

Diametral pitch P: the number of teeth per inch of pitch diameter, P = z/d with d in inches. It is the inch-system size index, related to the module by m = 25.4/P; a 10-pitch gear has m = 2.54 mm. Note p × P = π.

Pressure angle φ: the angle between the line of action (the common normal to the teeth, tangent to both base circles) and the common tangent to the pitch circles at the pitch point. 20° is the standard; 14½° is old practice and 25° is used for some heavy-duty gears. The base circle diameter is db = d cos φ.

Addendum ha: the radial height of the tooth above the pitch circle, m for standard 20° full-depth teeth, so the tip (addendum) circle is da = d + 2m. Dedendum hf: the radial depth below the pitch circle, 1.25m, so the root circle is df = d − 2.5m. The extra 0.25m is the clearance between the tip of one gear and the root of the other.

Backlash: the gap between the non-driving flanks of a meshing pair, measured on the pitch circle. It is made by thinning the teeth slightly so the pair does not jam through heat growth, errors and oil film; too much backlash gives knocking when the load reverses.

Contact ratio: the average number of tooth pairs in contact, equal to the path of contact divided by the base pitch πm cos φ (or the arc of contact divided by p). It must exceed 1 for smooth transfer of load; 1.4 to 1.8 is usual for spur gears.
Worked check. For z1 = 20, z2 = 60, m = 4 mm, φ = 20°: d1 = 80 mm, d2 = 240 mm, p = 12.57 mm, da1 = 88 mm, df1 = 70 mm, base pitch 11.81 mm, path of contact 19.73 mm and contact ratio 1.67.

bank.q: A gear material must supply core strength, surface hardness and machinability at acceptable cost. Discuss how through-hardened steel, case-carburised steel, cast iron and phosphor bronze meet these needs, and explain why the pinion is made harder than the gear.
outline: Core strength resists root bending; surface hardness resists pitting
Through-hardened carbon and alloy steels: simple, 250–350 BHN
Case carburising: hard case, tough core, grinding needed
Cast iron: cheap, quiet, weak in tension and shock; bronze for worm wheels
Pinion harder because it sees ratio-times more cycles; K = 0.16(BHN/100)²

answer.text: The three needs. Bending fatigue starts at the root fillet, where the whole tooth section carries the load, so the core must be strong and tough. Pitting starts on the flanks under repeated contact stress, so the surface must be hard. The gear must also be machinable and keep its shape through heat treatment, at a cost that suits the duty.

Through-hardened steels (C45, 40C8, 40Cr1, 42CrMo4). The whole gear is hardened and tempered to 250 to 350 BHN. Core and surface have the same hardness, so the tooth is tough and the process is cheap, and the gear can be cut after treatment. Above about 350 BHN cutting becomes hard and distortion grows, so the surface hardness, and with it the wear capacity, is limited. Typical allowable bending stress σb = σut/3, about 200 N/mm² for σut = 600 N/mm².

Case-carburised steels (20MnCr5, 15Ni4Cr1). Carbon is diffused 0.8 to 1.5 mm into a low-carbon alloy steel at about 900 to 930 °C, then the gear is quenched and tempered: case 58 to 62 HRC, core 30 to 40 HRC. This gives the best of both needs, a very hard flank and a tough core, so it is used for heavy load, shock and high speed (vehicle gearboxes). The price is distortion: the teeth must be ground after hardening, which adds cost. Nitriding and induction hardening are other ways to harden only the surface.

Grey cast iron (FG 200, FG 260). Cheap, casts to shape, machines well and damps noise, and its graphite helps it run with little lubrication. Its tensile and shock strength are low, so it suits large, slow, lightly loaded wheels running with a steel pinion, never a small high-speed pinion.

Phosphor bronze is used for worm wheels. The worm slides on the wheel, so the wheel must be conformable and resist seizure against a hard, ground steel worm. Non-metals (nylon, laminates) serve quiet, light drives.

Why the pinion is harder. With ratio i, each pinion tooth is loaded i times as often as a gear tooth. For a 20/60 pair at 1440 rpm for 10 000 h the pinion sees 60 × 1440 × 10 000 = 8.64 × 10⁸ cycles and the gear 2.88 × 10⁸. Equal hardness would make the pinion pit first, so a through-hardened pinion is made about 30 to 50 BHN harder (for example 300 BHN pinion, 250 BHN gear).

Effect on design numbers. The wear factor K = 0.16(BHN/100)² rises from 1.44 N/mm² at 300 BHN to 2.31 N/mm² at 380 BHN, a 60 % rise in wear strength for the same size. Hence the rule: if bending governs, use more module or a stronger core; if wear governs, use a harder surface.

bank.q: Explain why a helical gear pair carries more load and runs quieter than a spur pair of the same size and material. Define helix angle, normal module and transverse module, and calculate the force components for m<sub>n</sub> = 3 mm, z<sub>1</sub> = 20, ψ = 15°, φ<sub>n</sub> = 20°, 11 kW at 1450 rpm.
outline: Gradual engagement across the face; overlap ratio above 1; longer contact lines
ψ, m<sub>n</sub> (standard), m<sub>t</sub> = m<sub>n</sub>/cos ψ, z<sub>v</sub> = z/cos³ψ
F<sub>t</sub> = P/v, F<sub>a</sub> = F<sub>t</sub> tan ψ, F<sub>r</sub> = F<sub>t</sub> tan φ<sub>n</sub>/cos ψ
Thrust needs angular contact or taper roller bearings, or a herringbone gear

answer.text: Why quieter and stronger. A spur tooth meets its mate along the whole face width at once, so each tooth pair takes up load suddenly and the load jumps between one and two pairs. A helical tooth meets its mate at one end of the face and the contact line sweeps across it, so load is taken up gradually. With overlap ratio b sin ψ/(πmn) above 1, another tooth is always in contact somewhere along the face, so the total contact line is longer and changes little.

For strength, the tooth section in the normal plane is that of a larger spur gear with z<sub>v</sub> = z/cos³ψ teeth, which has a larger form factor, and the load is shared over more contact. For the same size and material the helical pair therefore carries more load, with less dynamic load, so a larger velocity factor C<sub>v</sub> = 5.6/(5.6 + √v) is used instead of 3/(3 + v).

Definitions. Helix angle ψ: the angle between a tooth and the shaft axis, measured on the pitch cylinder. Normal module mn: the module in the plane normal to the tooth, the standard (cutter) value. Transverse module mt: the module in the plane perpendicular to the axis, mt = mn/cos ψ; the pitch diameter is d = mt z.

The cost: thrust. Fa = 625 N pushes the shaft along its axis. One bearing on each shaft must take it: an angular contact ball bearing or a taper roller bearing, with the other bearing free to float. The thrust also reverses with the direction of rotation. Larger helix angles give more overlap but more thrust, so 15° to 25° is usual; a double helical (herringbone) gear cancels the thrust inside the gear and allows 30° to 45°.
Check. Resultant tooth force = √(2332² + 625² + 879²) = 2569 N, about 10 % more than Ft alone; the extra is mostly the thrust and the separating force that the bearings, not the teeth, must carry.

bank.q: A motor delivers 7.5 kW at 1440 rpm to a spur pinion of 20 teeth driving a gear of 80 teeth (20° full depth). Both are steel with σ<sub>ut</sub> = 600 N/mm² and 350 BHN surfaces; service factor 1.25, factor of safety 1.5, b = 10m, C<sub>v</sub> = 3/(3 + v). Find the module by the Lewis equation, then check the pair by Buckingham with e = 0.012 mm and C = 11 400 N/mm², and state which check governs.
outline: Weaker member from σ<sub>b</sub> Y
F<sub>t</sub> and v in terms of m; Lewis with C<sub>v</sub>; standard module
Buckingham dynamic load and effective load
Wear strength with Q and K
Factors of safety and the governing check

answer.text: Weaker member. Same material, so compare Y: Y1 = 0.484 − 2.87/20 = 0.3405, Y2 = 0.484 − 2.87/80 = 0.4481. The pinion is weaker; design it. σb = σut/3 = 200 N/mm².
Load in terms of m. d1 = 20m mm, v = π(0.020m)(1440)/60 = 1.508m m/s, Ft = 7500/(1.508m) = 4974/m N. Beam strength Sb = σb b m Y = 200 × 10m × m × 0.3405 = 681m² N.
Lewis sizing. Required Sb = fs Cs Ft/Cv.

Solving exactly gives m = 3.32 mm, so the first-choice standard module is m = 4 mm. Then b = 40 mm, d<sub>1</sub> = 80 mm, d<sub>2</sub> = 320 mm, a = 200 mm, v = 6.032 m/s and F<sub>t</sub> = 1243 N.
Buckingham dynamic load.
Bending check. Sb/Feff = 10 896/5632 = 1.93 ≥ 1.5: safe.

Which governs. Both checks pass; wear has the smaller margin (1.78 against 1.93), so wear governs and a softer surface would fail first: at 300 BHN, K = 1.44 and Sw = 7373 N, a factor of only 1.31. The design: m = 4 mm, b = 40 mm, z = 20/80, 350 BHN surfaces, pinion preferably 30 to 50 BHN harder than the gear because it sees four times the cycles.

bank.q: Design a helical pair to transmit 15 kW at 1000 rpm of the pinion with ratio 3.5 and helix angle 20°: z<sub>1</sub> = 20, φ<sub>n</sub> = 20°, steel with σ<sub>b</sub> = 200 N/mm² and 350 BHN, service factor 1.25, factor of safety 1.5, b = 10m<sub>n</sub>. Size m<sub>n</sub> by the Lewis equation (C<sub>v</sub> = 5.6/(5.6 + √v)), check by Buckingham (e = 0.010 mm, C = 11 400 N/mm²) and wear, and find the bearing forces.
outline: z<sub>2</sub> = 70, z<sub>v</sub> = z/cos³ψ, Y for z<sub>v</sub>
m<sub>n</sub> by trial with C<sub>v</sub>
Buckingham for helical gears with cos²ψ and cos ψ
Wear S<sub>w</sub> = b Q d<sub>1</sub> K/cos²ψ
Raise b if a check is marginal
F<sub>t</sub>, F<sub>a</sub>, F<sub>r</sub> for bearings

answer.text: Teeth. z2 = 3.5 × 20 = 70. cos 20° = 0.93969, cos³20° = 0.82976, so zv1 = 20/0.82976 = 24.10 and Y1 = 0.484 − 2.87/24.10 = 0.3649 (the gear, zv2 = 84.4, has a larger Y, so the pinion governs).
Lewis sizing. d1 = 20mn/0.93969 = 21.28mn mm; v = π d1 n/60 000; Sb = σb b mn Y = 200 × 10mn × mn × 0.3649.
Take m<sub>n</sub> = 4 mm: m<sub>t</sub> = 4.257 mm, d<sub>1</sub> = 85.13 mm, d<sub>2</sub> = 297.97 mm, a = 191.55 mm, b = 40 mm, F<sub>t</sub> = 3365 N.
Raise the face width to 45 mm (11.25mn, still within 10 to 15mn) and check again:

Bearing forces on the pinion. Fa = Ft tan ψ = 3365 × 0.36397 = 1225 N; Fr = Ft tan φn/cos ψ = 3365 × 0.36397/0.93969 = 1303 N. The axial thrust is about a third of Ft, so each shaft needs one angular contact or taper roller bearing to locate it.

Result. mn = 4 mm, ψ = 20°, z = 20/70, b = 45 mm, a = 191.55 mm; factors 1.64 in bending and 1.65 in wear; overlap ratio 45 × sin 20°/(4π) = 1.22. A larger helix angle would add overlap but raise Fa = Ft tan ψ.

bank.q: Design a straight bevel pair for a right-angle drive transmitting 4 kW at 900 rpm of the pinion, ratio 2.5, z<sub>1</sub> = 20, φ = 20°. Both gears are steel, σ<sub>b</sub> = 200 N/mm², 350 BHN; C<sub>s</sub> = 1.25, f<sub>s</sub> = 1.5, C<sub>v</sub> = 3/(3 + v), b = R/3 or 10m (the smaller), e = 0.010 mm, C = 11 400 N/mm². Find the module, check bending and wear, and find the bearing forces.
outline: Pitch angles and virtual teeth
Torque at the mean radius
S<sub>b</sub> = σ<sub>b</sub> b m Y(1 − b/R) and Lewis sizing
Buckingham and F<sub>eff</sub>
Wear with Q′ and the 0.75 factor
Axial and radial forces

answer.text: Lewis sizing. For each trial module: R = √((d1/2)² + (d2/2)²), b = smaller of R/3 and 10m, rm1 = d1/2 − (b sin γ1)/2, Ft = T/rm1, v at the large end.
Buckingham.

Forces for the bearings. Pinion: Fa1 = Ft tan φ sin γ1 = 1267 × 0.36397 × 0.37139 = 171 N (away from the apex); Fr1 = 1267 × 0.36397 × 0.92848 = 428 N. Gear: axial 428 N, radial 171 N. The pinion shaft also carries the 1267 N tangential force.

Result. m = 4 mm, z = 20/50, b = 35 mm, R = 107.70 mm; bending factor 1.53 (governs) and wear factor 1.77. Bending governs here because the bevel tooth loses strength towards the apex (the 0.675 factor), so a harder surface would not help; a larger module would.

bank.q: A single-start worm (m = 5 mm, d<sub>1</sub> = 50 mm) runs at 1440 rpm and drives a 40-tooth wheel, transmitting 2.5 kW; μ = 0.05, α<sub>n</sub> = 20°. Find the lead angle, rubbing velocity, efficiency, wheel torque and heat lost, and decide whether a housing of 0.75 m² with k = 16 W/(m²K) in still air at 35 °C is enough.
outline: q = d<sub>1</sub>/m, tan λ = z<sub>1</sub>/q
v<sub>s</sub> = v<sub>1</sub>/cos λ
η with α<sub>n</sub>, compared with tan λ/tan(λ + φ)
Heat (1 − η)P = kA(t − t<sub>0</sub>)
Conclusion: fins, fan or cooler

answer.text: Lead angle. q = d1/m = 50/5 = 10; tan λ = z1/q = 0.1, so λ = 5.71°. Lead L = πm = 15.71 mm; speed ratio 40, wheel speed 36 rpm; d2 = 200 mm, a = 125 mm.
Rubbing velocity. v1 = π × 0.050 × 1440/60 = 3.770 m/s; vs = 3.770/cos 5.71° = 3.789 m/s.
Efficiency.
Self-locking? φ = 2.86° < λ = 5.71°, so the drive is not self-locking; the wheel can back-drive the worm.

Torques and forces. T1 = 2500/(2π × 1440/60) = 16.58 N·m; Ft1 = 2T1/d1 = 663 N. T2 = ηP/ω2 = 0.649 × 2500/(2π × 36/60) = 430.5 N·m; Ft2 = 2T2/d2 = 4305 N, which is also the axial thrust on the worm bearings.

Separating force. Fr = Ft1 sin αn/(cos αn sin λ + μ cos λ) = 663 × 0.34202/(0.93969 × 0.09950 + 0.05 × 0.99504) = 226.8/0.14325 = 1583 N, pushing the worm and wheel shafts apart. The worm bearings therefore see 4305 N of thrust and 1583 N plus 663 N across the shaft.
Power check. Output = T2 ω2 = 430.5 × 2π × 36/60 = 1623 W = 0.649 × 2500 W, so 877 W is lost in the mesh, matching the heat figure below.
Heat. Loss = (1 − η)P = (1 − 0.649) × 2500 = 877 W. Still air: t − t0 = 877/(16 × 0.75) = 73.1 K, so the oil would reach 35 + 73 = 108 °C, well above the usual limit of about 80 °C.

Decision. Natural cooling is not enough. A fan on the worm shaft that raises k to about 30 W/(m²K) gives t − t0 = 877/(30 × 0.75) = 39 K and oil at 74 °C, which is acceptable; fins, a larger housing or a two-start worm (higher λ, higher η) are the other choices. Most of the input (35 %) becomes heat because the lead angle is small, which is the price of a 40:1 reduction in one stage. A two-start worm with the same q would have tan λ = 0.2, λ = 11.31° and η = (0.93969 − 0.05 × 0.2)/(0.93969 + 0.05 × 5) = 0.781, but the ratio would fall to 20.

bank.q: A planetary train has a sun of 20 teeth, planets of 30 teeth and a fixed annulus of 80 teeth. The sun runs at 1000 rpm. By the tabular method find the arm speed, the planet speed and its spin on the pin, the speed ratio, and the holding torque on the annulus when the sun takes 5 kW.
outline: Geometry check z<sub>R</sub> = z<sub>S</sub> + 2z<sub>P</sub>
Table: arm fixed, sun +x; add y
Annulus fixed gives y = x z<sub>S</sub>/z<sub>R</sub>
Arm and planet speeds
Torque and power balance

answer.text: Geometry. zS + 2zP = 20 + 60 = 80 = zR, so the planets fit.
Table. Counter-clockwise positive.
Conditions. Annulus fixed: y − 0.25x = 0, so y = 0.25x. Sun at 1000 rpm: x + y = 1000, so 1.25x = 1000, x = 800, y = 200.

Speeds. Arm = y = 200 rpm, in the sun's direction. Planet = y − 0.6667x = 200 − 533.3 = −333.3 rpm, opposite to the sun. Its spin on the pin, relative to the arm, is −333.3 − 200 = −533.3 rpm. Speed ratio = 1000/200 = 5 = 1 + zR/zS, the train value 1/5.

Torques. TS = 5000/(2π × 1000/60) = 47.75 N·m. Power balance with no loss: TA × 200 = −47.75 × 1000, so TA = −238.7 N·m (the load resists the arm with 238.7 N·m, five times the input). Torque balance: TR = −(TS + TA) = −(47.75 − 238.7) = 191.0 N·m, the torque the annulus mounting must hold.
Check by the relative-speed relation. (nR − nA)/(nS − nA) = −zS/zR: (0 − 200)/(1000 − 200) = −0.25 = −20/80. Correct.
Number of planets. Equal spacing needs (zS + zR)/n to be a whole number. (20 + 80)/3 = 33.3, so three planets cannot be spaced equally; (20 + 80)/4 = 25, so use four planets at 90°.

Planet loads. Take m = 3 mm: sun radius rS = 30 mm, planet radius 45 mm, arm radius rS + rP = 75 mm. Tangential force at each sun mesh = TS/(4 rS) = 47.75/(4 × 0.030) = 397.9 N. The ring pushes the planet with an equal force in the same direction, so each planet pin carries 2 × 397.9 = 795.8 N.
Check on the arm. 4 × 795.8 N × 0.075 m = 238.7 N·m, equal to TA. Output power = 238.7 × 2π × 200/60 = 5000 W, equal to the input, as it must be with no loss.

bank.q: A machine tool spindle needs six speeds from 100 rpm to 1000 rpm in geometric progression. Choose the step ratio, the structure and the group order, draw the ray diagram, and fix the tooth numbers of each pair with one module so that the shaft centre distances are equal.
outline: Structure 3(1) 2(3); limits 1/4 and 2 per pair
Ray diagram on log scale
Equal tooth sums in a group; speed check and deviation

answer.text: Step ratio. φ = (1000/100)1/5 = 100.2 = 1.585, so the standard value 1.58 (the R5 series) fits. Standard speeds: 100, 160, 250, 400, 630, 1000 rpm.

Structure. 6 = 3 × 2 or 2 × 3. Choose 6 = 3(1) 2(3): the group nearer the motor has more ratios and the small steps, which keeps the faster shafts carrying more gears but smaller torques. Group b then spans φ³ = 3.95, within the limit of 4 for a reduction.

Group ratios. Shaft I runs at 1000 rpm. Group a (I to II): 1, 1/1.58, 1/2.5, giving 1000, 630, 400 rpm on shaft II. Group b (II to III): 1 and 1/3.95 (use 1/4), giving 1000, 630, 400 and 250, 160, 100 rpm on shaft III.
Ray diagram. Three vertical shaft lines I, II, III; six equally spaced horizontal lines for 100 to 1000 rpm.

Tooth numbers. Group a with sum 70: 1:1 gives 35/35; 1:1.58 gives 70/2.58 = 27.1, so 27/43; 1:2.5 gives 70/3.5 = 20, so 20/50. Group b with sum 100: 1:1 gives 50/50; 1:4 gives 20/80. All gears have 20 or more teeth, above the undercut limit.
Speed check.

Conclusion. All deviations are inside ±10(φ − 1) % = ±5.8 %. Every pair keeps within a reduction of 1/4 and no step-up is needed. In the gearing diagram the three group-a gears on shaft I form a sliding cluster, and the two group-b gears on shaft III another.

Why not the other orders. With 6 = 2(1) 3(2), group b would need 1, 1/φ² and 1/φ⁴ = 1/6.25, beyond the 1/4 limit; it could only be met with a step-up pair. With 6 = 3(2) 2(1), group a would span φ⁴ = 6.25, which has the same problem. So 3(1) 2(3) is the only order that stays inside the limits with reductions alone.

Centre distances. With m = 3 mm, every pair in group a has the sum 70 and a = 3 × 70/2 = 105 mm; every pair in group b has the sum 100 and a = 3 × 100/2 = 150 mm. Equal sums inside a group are what let all the pairs of that group share one pair of shafts. The box has ten gears in all: six in group a and four in group b.

bank.q: Bending fatigue at the root and pitting of the flank are the two competing limits on a spur gear. Compare them in terms of where the stress acts, what resists each, and how load, speed and surface hardness decide which one governs. Use the pair m = 4 mm, b = 40 mm, z = 20/60, 10 kW at 1200 rpm to illustrate.
outline: Bending: tensile stress at the root fillet, resisted by core strength; S<sub>b</sub> = σ<sub>b</sub> b m Y
Pitting: contact stress on the flank, resisted by surface hardness; S<sub>w</sub> = b Q d<sub>1</sub> K
Speed raises the dynamic load for both
Numbers: bending 1.52, wear 0.97 at 300 BHN, 1.55 at 380 BHN
Design response for each

answer.text: Where the stress acts. Bending: the tooth is a cantilever and the largest tensile stress is at the root fillet on the loaded side; fatigue cracks start there and the tooth breaks off. Pitting: the flanks are pressed together under Hertz contact stress, highest just below the surface near the pitch line; repeated cycles start fine cracks that lift out small pits, then the flank wears and gets noisy.

What resists each. Bending depends on the strength and toughness of the core and on tooth size: Sb = σb b m Y grows with the module. Pitting depends on surface hardness and on the radii of curvature: Sw = b Q d1 K, with K = 0.16(BHN/100)², grows with the pinion diameter and the square of the hardness, but not with the module directly.

Effect of load and speed. Both checks are made against Feff = Cs Ft + Fd. Higher speed raises Buckingham's Fd for both. Higher torque raises Ft for both. Contact damage grows with about the cube of the load, so a load spectrum shifts the balance towards pitting.
Illustration. For the pair (v = 5.027 m/s, Ft = 1989 N, e = 0.015 mm, Cs = 1.25): Fd = 4671 N and Feff = 7158 N.

Reading it. At 300 BHN the root is safe but the flanks would pit: wear governs. Raising the surface hardness to 380 BHN multiplies K by 1.6 and makes wear safe without touching the module. If instead bending had failed, a larger module or wider face, or a tougher core, would be the cure; a harder case does little for the root.

How the balance moves. Case hardening (58 to 62 HRC) raises K so much that bending becomes the limit; then the designer raises the module or shot-peens the root. Through-hardened gears at high load usually stay wear-limited. Small, fine-pitch pinions with many teeth are bending-limited; large, slow, heavily loaded gears are wear-limited.
Conclusion. Check both every time, report the smaller factor of safety, and cure each limit with its own remedy: module and core for bending, hardness and diameter for pitting.

bank.q: A crane gearbox runs at constant speed and carries 20 kW for 10 % of its life and 8 kW for 90 %. Using Miner's rule with a contact life exponent of 3, find the equivalent power. Evaluate what happens to the equivalent power and to the life of the same gears if the heavy lifts become 20 % of the time.
outline: F<sup>k</sup> N = constant; Miner D = Σ n<sub>i</sub>/N<sub>i</sub>
P<sub>eq</sub> = (Σ p<sub>i</sub> P<sub>i</sub>³)<sup>1/3</sup>
Numbers for 10 % and 20 %
Life ∝ P<sub>eq</sub><sup>−3</sup>
Design response

answer.text: Basis. Along the sloping part of the S-N curve, Pk N = constant, with k = 3 for contact fatigue. Miner's rule adds the damage fractions D = Σ ni/Ni and predicts failure at D = 1.
Equivalent load. At constant speed the cycle fractions equal the time fractions pi. A steady Peq for the same total cycles gives the same damage when Peq³ = Σ pi Pi³, so Peq = (Σ pi Pi³)1/3.
Present duty.
Heavy lifts at 20 %.

Effect on life. For the same gears, life ∝ Peq−3: (10.80/12.62)³ = 0.627. Doubling the share of heavy lifts raises the equivalent load by only 17 % but cuts the contact life by 37 %. A gearbox designed for 20 000 h would now last about 12 500 h.

Evaluation. The equivalent load is dominated by the heavy lifts: 10 % of the time at 20 kW causes 63 % of the damage (800 of 1260.8). The simple average (9.2 kW) would under-size the gears; the maximum (20 kW) would over-size them badly. Bending uses a larger exponent, so the heavy lifts dominate it even more.

Design response. Either size for the new Peq (wear strength must rise by 12.62/10.80 = 1.17, for example from 350 to about 380 BHN, since K ∝ BHN² and 1.17 × 1.96 = 2.29), or keep the gears and shorten the inspection and replacement interval, backed by oil analysis to catch pitting early.

Share of damage at 20 %. The heavy lifts now cause 1600/2009.6 = 80 % of the damage, against 63 % before. Life in cycles: a pinion at 1440 rpm for 20 000 h makes 1440 × 60 × 20 000 = 1.73 × 10⁹ cycles; at 0.627 of that life it reaches only about 1.08 × 10⁹ cycles at the higher Peq.

bank.q: A conveyor needs a 20:1 reduction from a 10 kW, 1440 rpm motor in two spur stages. Discuss how you would split the ratio, choose materials, carry the torques forward, check the heat for a 1.0 m² housing (k = 15 W/(m²K), air at 35 °C), and use a speed chart for a two-speed version whose second output speed is one standard step above 72 rpm.
outline: Split: equal √20 = 4.47 or a slightly larger first stage
Tooth numbers and speeds
Torques with 98 % per stage
Materials per stage
Bearings and heat
Two-speed version: change gears in stage 1 and the speed chart

answer.text: Ratio split. i = 1440/72 = 20. An equal split, √20 = 4.47, makes the two stages similar; a slightly larger first-stage ratio keeps the two large wheels a similar size so both dip in the oil. Choose stage 1 = 20/90 (4.5) and stage 2 = 18/80 (4.444): overall 20.0, shafts at 1440, 320 and 72 rpm.

Torques forward with losses. T1 = 10 000/(2π × 1440/60) = 66.3 N·m; T2 = 66.3 × 4.5 × 0.98 = 292.4 N·m; T3 = 292.4 × 4.444 × 0.98 = 1273.8 N·m. The second stage carries 4.4 times the torque of the first, so its module and face width are larger; each stage is designed with its own torque.

Materials. Stage 1 runs fast with small torque: through-hardened C45 or 40C8 (pinion about 300 BHN, gear about 250 BHN) is enough. Stage 2 runs slowly with large torque and is usually wear-limited, so a surface-hardened or case-carburised pinion with a through-hardened alloy steel gear keeps the box small. Helical teeth would make it quieter, at the cost of thrust bearings.

Bearings. Each shaft carries the tooth forces of its gears (tangential T/r and radial Ft tan φ); with helical gears add Fa = Ft tan ψ and locate each shaft with one bearing able to take thrust. Bearing life is checked at the shaft's own speed; the slow output shaft needs large bearings for its load but few revolutions.
Heat. η = 0.98² = 0.9604; heat = 10 000 × 0.0396 = 396 W; t − t0 = 396/(15 × 1.0) = 26.4 K; oil at 61.4 °C, below about 80 °C, so splash lubrication and natural cooling are enough.

Two-speed version. One standard step above 72 rpm with φ = 1.26 is about 90 rpm. Add a second pair to stage 1 with the same tooth sum, 110: 24/86 gives 3.583. Output = 1440/3.583/4.444 = 90.4 rpm, and 90.4/72 = 1.256 ≈ 1.26. The two stage-1 pairs form a sliding cluster on shaft 1.

Speed chart reading. Two rays leave 1440 rpm on shaft 1 and reach 402 and 320 rpm on shaft 2; one parallel pair of rays (the same 18/80 ratio) carries them to 90.4 and 72 rpm. The rays do not land on the same speed, so the two outputs are distinct.

Conclusion. Stage ratios 4.5 and 4.444 (or 3.583 for the higher speed), torques 66.3, 292.4 and 1273.8 N·m at the lower speed, oil at about 61 °C. Check that the second stage's gears also meet the higher shaft-2 speed of 402 rpm, at which their dynamic load is larger.

bank.q: Compare an epicyclic gear train with a sliding-gear train for the spindle drive of a machine tool. Cover the speeds obtainable, the number of gear pairs needed, compactness, efficiency and manufacture, and state which you would choose for six spindle speeds from 100 to 560 rpm.
outline: Sliding-gear box: geometric steps from groups in series, one pair per speed path
Epicyclic: large ratio in a small coaxial box, ratios by holding members with clutches or brakes
Pairs and compactness
Efficiency and manufacture
Recommendation for 6 speeds

answer.text: Speeds. A sliding-gear box gives exactly the geometric series the designer chooses: groups in series multiply the ratios, 3 × 2 = 6 speeds. An epicyclic set gives a few fixed ratios per set, depending on which member is held: with zS = 24, zR = 60, ring fixed gives 1 + 60/24 = 3.5, sun fixed gives 1 + 24/60 = 1.4, and locking two members gives 1. Six geometric speeds need two or three sets with clutches and brakes.

Number of gear pairs. For 6 = 3(1) 2(3) with φ = 1.41 the sliding box needs five pairs (36/36, 30/42, 24/48; 38/38, 20/56), ten gears on three shafts. An epicyclic solution needs a sun, three planets and a ring per set, plus clutches and brakes for each ratio.

Compactness. The epicyclic set is coaxial and shares the load among three planets, so it carries more torque in a smaller diameter and is ideal where space is tight (wheel hubs, automatic gearboxes). The sliding box needs three parallel shafts and a larger housing, but the space is usually available in a machine-tool headstock.

Efficiency. Each spur pair loses about 2 %; a speed path through two pairs is about 96 % efficient. An epicyclic set has more meshes in parallel plus planet bearing and clutch drag losses, which are similar at the ratios a machine tool needs.

Manufacture and use. Sliding gears are ordinary spur gears, cheap to make, easy to service, but shifted only when the spindle is stopped. Epicyclic sets need accurate internal gears, careful planet spacing ((zS + zR)/number of planets a whole number) and clutches, but can change ratio under load, which matters for automatic drives.

Recommendation. For six speeds from 100 to 560 rpm on a conventional machine tool, the sliding-gear box is the better choice: it gives the exact standard speeds 100, 140, 200, 280, 400, 560 with five simple pairs, costs less and is easy to repair; shifting at rest is acceptable. Choose epicyclic sets only where the drive must be coaxial and compact or must shift under load.

Size check. With m = 3 mm, the epicyclic set zS = 24, zP = 18, zR = 60 gives 3.5 inside a ring of pitch diameter 180 mm, all on one axis; three planets fit because (24 + 60)/3 = 28. A single spur pair for 3.5, for example 20/70 at m = 3 mm, needs a centre distance of 135 mm and an overall width of 30 + 135 + 105 = 270 mm. The epicyclic set is about two-thirds the width and puts the output on the input axis.

glossary.def: A toothed wheel that transmits motion and torque to another by successive contact of teeth.
The smaller gear of a meshing pair, usually the driver.
The imaginary circle on which two meshing gears roll without slipping; the ratio and the module are based on it.
The pitch circle diameter in mm divided by the number of teeth; the size index of gear teeth.
The arc on the pitch circle from a point on one tooth to the same point on the next, equal to π times the module.
The angle between the line of action and the common tangent to the pitch circles, usually 20°.
The radial height of a tooth above the pitch circle, one module for standard teeth.
The radial depth of a tooth below the pitch circle, 1.25 module for standard full-depth teeth.
The gap between the non-driving flanks of meshing teeth.
The curve traced by the end of a taut string unwound from a base circle; its normal is always tangent to the base circle.
The average number of tooth pairs in contact: the path of contact divided by the base pitch.
Removal of metal at the root of a pinion with too few teeth during cutting, which weakens the tooth; it is the damage caused by interference.
A number that depends on the tooth form and number of teeth and gives the bending strength of the tooth treated as a cantilever.
The largest tangential load a tooth can carry in bending at the allowable stress.
A factor below 1 that allows for the dynamic load of tooth errors at speed in the first sizing of a gear.
A factor above 1 that allows for shock and the character of the driver and the driven machine.
The extra tooth load caused by tooth errors and impact at running speed, estimated by Buckingham's equation.
The largest tangential load the tooth flanks can carry without pitting over a long life.
Fatigue failure of the tooth surface, seen as small craters on the flank.
The angle a helical tooth makes with the shaft axis.
The tooth count of the equivalent spur gear used in strength formulas for helical and bevel gears.
The cone at the large end of a bevel gear whose elements are perpendicular to the pitch cone; unrolled, it shows the teeth as spur teeth.
The ratio of worm pitch diameter to module, q = d/m.
The state of a worm drive in which the wheel cannot drive the worm, roughly when the lead angle is less than the friction angle.
A train in which planet gears carried by an arm roll round a central sun gear, usually inside a ring gear.
A single steady load that causes the same fatigue damage as a varying load over the same number of cycles.
A speed chart on a log scale in which each gear pair is a straight ray between two shafts.
The constant factor between consecutive spindle speeds of a geometric series.
The number of speeds written as a product of the number of ratios in each gear group, with each group characteristic.
